title: Wisconsin Measles Outbreak Hits 39 Cases as Three Counties Report Spread
excerpt: The fast-growing cluster in southwest Wisconsin has nearly doubled in days, with almost all cases among unvaccinated residents in a state with the second-lowest kindergarten vaccination rate in the U.S.
body:
• Southwest Wisconsin's measles outbreak has grown to 39 cases across three counties, nearly doubling over the weekend of August 16–17
  • All but one of Wisconsin's 41 measles patients in 2026 were unvaccinated; two have been hospitalized
  • Wisconsin has the second-lowest kindergarten measles vaccination rate in the nation at 85%, behind only Idaho
  • The U.S. has recorded over 2,465 measles cases in 2026, the worst outbreak in decades, driven by declining vaccination rates

A measles outbreak in southwest Wisconsin has nearly doubled in size over a single weekend, with state data updated August 18 showing 39 cases tied to the cluster — up from 21 confirmed and probable cases reported just days earlier. The outbreak has now surpassed last year's cluster in Oconto County, making it the largest in the state in recent memory.

The fast-moving outbreak is concentrated in Iowa County but has expanded to two neighboring counties: six confirmed or probable cases in Lafayette County and two in Grant County. State epidemiologist Dr. Ryan Westergaard said the rapid emergence of cases among people who have not traveled outside Wisconsin indicates active local transmission.

Vaccination Gap at the Center

Of the 41 Wisconsin residents who have contracted measles in 2026 — including two earlier, unrelated cases in Dane and Waukesha counties — all but one had not received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two patients have been hospitalized, one in the current outbreak.

https://x.com/fox32news/status/2089447214770757894

The age breakdown underscores the vulnerability of unvaccinated children: just over half of cases are among those aged 5 to 17, while 39% are adults and 9.8% are children under 5.

New CDC data released August 17 spotlighted Wisconsin's lagging immunization coverage. Approximately 85% of Wisconsin kindergartners had been vaccinated against measles for the 2025–2026 school year — the second-lowest rate in the nation, behind only Idaho. The national average stands at 92.5%.

"The rapid emergence of these cases, particularly among people who have not traveled outside of Wisconsin, indicates that there is active local transmission."

— Dr. Ryan Westergaard, Wisconsin DHS Chief Medical Officer

National Context: Worst Outbreak in Decades

Wisconsin's outbreak is part of a national resurgence. The United States has recorded more than 2,465 measles cases across 48 states since early 2025, when an outbreak began in a rural Texas community with low vaccination rates. One in eight cases nationally has required hospitalization.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known — far more transmissible than COVID-19 or chickenpox. The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after an infected person coughs or sneezes, and can cause serious complications including pneumonia, brain swelling and deafness.

The MMR vaccine is 97% effective at preventing infection with two doses and 93% effective with one. Health officials say the outbreaks are driven almost entirely by declining vaccination rates, with more than 90% of cases nationally occurring among people who were either unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status.

No Public Exposure Sites Identified

Wisconsin health officials have not identified any public locations where people may have been exposed, and are conducting contact tracing confidentially. Cases in the region were first reported to the public on August 11, when two cases were confirmed in Iowa and Lafayette counties. State officials warned at the time that more unidentified cases were likely.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services is working with local health departments in all three affected counties and receiving support from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to investigate the cases, trace exposures and contain further spread.

What Indian-American Families Should Know

For Indian diaspora families with young children, the outbreak is a reminder to verify vaccination status — particularly for families who travel frequently between the U.S. and India, where measles remains endemic. The Wisconsin Immunization Registry allows residents to check their vaccine records online. Parents unsure whether their children have received both doses of the MMR vaccine should contact their healthcare provider.

Health officials recommend that anyone who thinks they may have measles avoid contact with others and call a doctor's office before visiting in person, to prevent potential transmission in waiting rooms.
